content.text: Which of the following diagrams represents the curve of induced emf against position?

content.alt_text: Option A: one complete sinusoidal cycle of induced emf against position, P at zero rising to a positive maximum at Q, zero at R, negative minimum at S, zero at T
Option B: induced emf starting at a positive maximum at P, zero at Q, negative minimum at R, zero at S, positive maximum at T
Option C: two complete sinusoidal cycles of induced emf against position over the interval P to T
Option D: induced emf starting at a positive maximum at P, falling through Q to a negative minimum, rising through S to a positive maximum at R and T

content.text: The induced emf depends on how fast the flux is changing, not on the flux itself: it is largest where the flux is changing fastest and zero where the flux is at a maximum or a minimum.
From the diagram, decide at which positions the plane of the coil contains $B$ and at which it is perpendicular to $B$, then remember that $P$ to $T$ is four quarter-turns of the coil.
B

The induced emf depends on how fast the flux is changing, $|\varepsilon| = N\left|\dfrac{\Delta \Phi}{\Delta t}\right|$, not on the flux itself. Where the flux is at a maximum or a minimum the emf is zero; where the flux is changing fastest the emf has its greatest magnitude.

From the figure the plane of the coil contains $B$ at $P$, $R$ and $T$, so the flux is zero at those three positions; at $Q$ and $S$ the coil has turned through a further $90^{\circ}$ and the flux is at its maximum magnitude. The emf is therefore zero at $Q$ and $S$ and has its maximum magnitude at $P$, $R$ and $T$.

The interval $P$ to $T$ spans four quarter-turns, so the emf completes one full cycle. It is at a positive maximum at $P$, falls through zero at $Q$, reaches its negative maximum at $R$, returns through zero at $S$ and is back at a positive maximum at $T$, since $P$ and $T$ are the same coil orientation a full turn apart - curve (B).

2. Hold the mass to the side to give a small angular displacement, $\theta$.
3. Release the mass and measure the time for one period ($T$).
4. Record the result in a table.
5. Repeat using a string length ($L$) of $0.09\,\mathrm{m}$ and continue until the string length is $0.19\,\mathrm{m}$ (going up in $0.01\,\mathrm{m}$ increments, using the same initial angular displacement each time).
6. Calculate $g$ using the relationship $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{L}{g}}$.
The results are shown in the table:

content.text: Outline TWO changes that could be made to the experimental procedure that would improve its accuracy.
(Note: the procedure as printed measures only one period for each length; maintaining a constant initial angular displacement does not by itself improve accuracy.)

Look at step 3 of the printed procedure. A single period at these lengths lasts about $0.6\,\mathrm{s}$, and a human reaction time is of order $0.2\,\mathrm{s}$, so most of what is being measured is reaction time. Decide what quantity you should actually be timing.

The second change should deal with the random scatter that survives at each length. Ask what you can do with several timings at the same length, and remember that a straight line drawn through all the results, as in part (c), is itself a way of averaging them.

Time many oscillations (e.g. 10 or 20 periods) and divide by that number, rather than timing a single period. Repeat the timing at each length and take an average (or plot $T^{2}$ against $L$ and use a line of best fit) rather than relying on a single measurement.

Two changes earn the two marks. First, time a large number of oscillations, 10, 20 or more, and divide the total time by that number: at $L = 0.08\,\mathrm{m}$, $T = 0.57\,\mathrm{s}$, so 10 oscillations take $5.7\,\mathrm{s}$ and a $0.2\,\mathrm{s}$ reaction error becomes 3.5% of the period instead of 35%, with the fractional uncertainty falling in proportion to the number of oscillations counted. Second, repeat the timing at each length and average it, or plot $T^{2}$ against $L$ and take a line of best fit, so that the random error in any one reading is spread over the whole data set instead of being carried into a single value of $g$.

Other acceptable changes, if these are not offered, are a light bob on a light inextensible string so the simple-pendulum approximation in $T = 2\pi\sqrt{L/g}$ is better satisfied; measuring $L$ from the pivot to the centre of mass of the bob rather than to the bottom of it; reading the length against a datum with a metre rule to remove parallax; and photogate or video timing instead of a stopwatch. Holding the initial angular displacement small and constant is necessary for the small-angle assumption but does not improve accuracy, so it cannot be one of the two changes the question asks for. One mark is for a single valid change.

content.text: Compare Kim's and Ali's methods of calculating $g$ and identify the better approach.

Kim computes a value of $g$ from each length separately and then averages, so every random error in every timing is carried straight into the answer. Ali's line of best fit is fitted to all twelve points at once. Ask which arrangement lets a single bad timing do the least damage.

It helps to be precise about what the gradient is. Since $T = 2\pi\sqrt{L/g}$ gives $T^{2} = \frac{4\pi^{2}}{g}L$, the gradient of that line is a single estimate of one number, so compare that with Kim's twelve separate estimates of the same number rather than judging the two methods in the abstract.

Kim calculated a mean value of $g$ from each individual data point, so random errors in every reading are carried through into the result. Ali plotted $T^{2}$ against $L$ and used the gradient of a line of best fit, which averages all the data and reduces the effect of random error. Ali's method is the better approach.

Since $T = 2\pi\sqrt{L/g}$, then $T^{2} = \dfrac{4\pi^{2}}{g}L$, so $T^{2}$ against $L$ is a straight line through the origin with gradient $4\pi^{2}/g$ and hence $g = \dfrac{4\pi^{2}}{\text{gradient}}$.

content.text: Describe TWO difficulties associated with effective or reliable communications between satellites and Earth.

The marks are for identifying a difficulty and then describing it, so name the mechanism as well as the effect. Ask what lies between the satellite and the ground that the signal has to get through, and then ask what has happened to the strength of the signal after such a long journey.

A third route is the propagation time: work out what a geostationary orbit does to the round-trip time for a signal, and what that rules out. Whichever you choose, say what the difficulty prevents or requires, not just what it is.

Atmospheric absorption: the signal must use a frequency band that is not absorbed by the ionosphere or water vapour, which limits the available bandwidth. Signal attenuation and noise: the signal is very weak after travelling tens of thousands of kilometres and is contaminated by background noise and interference, so error correction and high transmitter power are needed. (Other acceptable difficulties: the large time delay between transmission and reception, and the need for satellites to be in line of sight / geostationary positioning.)
Two difficulties, each identified and then described:

items: Atmospheric absorption. The ionosphere reflects radio waves below roughly $30\,\mathrm{MHz}$ and the gases in the atmosphere, particularly water vapour, absorb strongly at many infrared and optical wavelengths, so the signal must be sent in one of the narrow transmission windows such as the microwave band. Because the usable band is narrow, only a limited bandwidth is available, so only a small amount of information can be sent at a time.

Signal attenuation and noise. After travelling tens of thousands of kilometres the signal is extremely weak, and it arrives mixed with cosmic noise and interference from other transmitters and electrical equipment. A large transmitter power, high-gain directional antennas, low-noise receivers and error-correcting coding are therefore all needed, and a proportion of the transmitted energy is still lost before the signal is usable.

content.text: A third acceptable difficulty is propagation delay: a signal takes about $0.25\,\mathrm{s}$ to travel to a geostationary satellite and back, so real-time conversation is impossible, the link budget must allow a very large path loss, and satellites need large on-board storage and forwarding.

content.text: Justify the student's conclusion that: 'The boat can be regarded as an inertial frame of reference'.
Begin with the definition rather than the data: in an inertial frame of reference, an object on which no net force acts remains at rest or continues in a straight line at constant velocity.

Then read each row of the table as a test of that definition. Ask what force acted on the dropped ball and in which direction, and ask what the constant velocity of each rolled ball rules out about the motion of the boat — in particular, use the third row to check the fore-and-aft direction.

The boat did not accelerate: the ball dropped from a set height fell vertically with increasing velocity because the only force (and hence acceleration) acting on it was gravity, and balls rolled in any direction across the boat moved with constant velocity, so they exhibited no acceleration relative to the boat. An inertial frame of reference is one in which an object, if free of net force, remains at rest or moves with constant velocity; since all three observations are consistent with no acceleration of the boat, the boat is an inertial frame of reference.

An inertial frame of reference is one in which an object acted on by no net force remains at rest or moves with constant velocity in a straight line, so any acceleration seen in such a frame is due to a net force.

The dropped ball fell vertically, so the only force acting on it was its weight, and it accelerated downwards at $g$ because of gravity. It did not fall to one side, which shows the boat had no horizontal acceleration.

The balls rolled across the floor moved with constant velocity, in every direction tested, including from the back of the boat towards the front. Constant velocity in all directions means no net force acted on them in the boat's frame, so the boat was not accelerating. Since nothing on the boat exhibited an acceleration that could not be attributed to a net force, the boat was an inertial frame of reference and the student's conclusion is justified.

content.text: What is the function of the brush in a generator?

The brushes are the only electrical path between the rotating coil and the stationary external circuit. Say what they have to stay in contact with, and what would happen to the circuit, and to the current, if they were removed.
The brushes maintain a sliding electrical contact between the rotating coil (via the slip rings or the split-ring commutator) and the external circuit, collecting the induced current.

The ends of the rotating coil are joined to the slip rings, or to the two halves of the split-ring commutator, and those rings turn with the coil. The carbon brushes press against them and are held in place by springs, so they maintain a continuous sliding electrical contact and collect the induced current, carrying it from the rotating coil out to the external circuit. Because the contact is sliding rather than fixed, it survives the coil turning through every orientation; remove the brushes and the circuit is opened at two points a half rotation apart, so no current would flow at all. That collecting-and-maintaining-contact function is the single mark; naming the carbon, or naming the spring, is not what is being examined.

content.text: Which of these generators is a DC generator? Justify your choice.

Compare the two ring assemblies carefully in the diagram: $P$ has two complete rings and $Q$ has a single ring cut into two halves. Work out what each one does to the current as the coil turns through a half rotation.

The current in the coil itself is the same alternating current in both machines, so the difference must lie entirely in what happens to the connection to the external circuit at the moment that current reverses. Ask what an external circuit would receive if the coil's connections were never swapped.

Generator $Q$. The current induced in the rotating coil is alternating (it reverses every half rotation), but the split-ring commutator reverses the connection to the external circuit at the same instant, so the output is a unidirectional (direct) current. Generator $P$ has continuous slip rings, so it delivers AC.
The difference between $P$ and $Q$ is the ring assembly: $P$ uses slip rings (AC out), $Q$ uses a split-ring commutator (DC out).

content.text: Outline why AC generators are used in large-scale electrical power production.

For a fixed amount of power, $P = VI$, so the current in a transmission line is inversely proportional to the voltage used to send it. Then look at how the energy lost heating those lines depends on that current: $P_{\text{loss}} = I^{2}R$.

The catch is that changing the voltage of a supply requires a transformer, and a transformer does nothing at all to a steady DC supply. Decide which of the two quantities a power station can conveniently change, and whether that choice is available to it if it generates DC.

AC can be easily stepped up (and back down) using transformers. Stepping up the voltage for transmission (with a corresponding reduction in current for the same power, $P = VI$) greatly reduces the $I^2R$ energy loss as the power is transmitted from the power station to consumers, so large-scale generation and transmission are far more efficient with AC.

content.text: State Lenz's law.

This is a statement about the direction of an induced current. Write it as 'the induced current flows in a direction such that it...', and make sure the thing it opposes is the CHANGE in magnetic flux, not the flux itself and not the motion of the circuit.
The induced current flows in a direction such that it opposes the change in magnetic flux that produced it.

Lenz's law states that the induced current flows in a direction such that it opposes the change in magnetic flux that produced it. Both halves of that sentence are load-bearing. It is the change in flux that is opposed, not the flux: a rod moving into a stronger field still has an induced current flowing so as to oppose the increase, and a rod moving out of a field has a current that opposes the decrease. And the opposition is exerted by the magnetic field that the induced current itself creates, which is why the law is entirely consistent with conservation of energy rather than a contradiction of it, since the work an external agent does in producing the change in flux is exactly the energy dissipated in the circuit. Statements that the induced current opposes the field, or opposes the motion, or flows to oppose the magnet, miss the change and do not earn the mark. The one mark is for an accurate statement of the law.

content.text: When the metal rod is moved upwards through the magnetic field as shown in the diagram, an emf is induced between the two ends.

For (b)(i): write down the direction of $\mathbf{v}$ and the direction of $\mathbf{B}$ - the field in the gap runs from the $N$ face of the left magnet to the $S$ face of the right magnet - and then use $\mathbf{F} = q\mathbf{v}\times\mathbf{B}$ with the sign of the charge carried by the current carriers in a metal in mind. Which end of the rod collects them?

For (b)(ii): an emf here is a separation of charge, not a flow of current. Say what force acts on the free charge carriers in the moving rod, in which direction along the rod it acts, and what that does to the distribution of positive and negative charge. The separation stops when the electric force from the separated charge just balances the magnetic force.

(i) End $X$ is negative and end $Y$ is positive. (ii) The rod moves upwards through the horizontal magnetic field, so the flux linking it changes and an emf is induced in it. The free charge carriers in the rod move with the rod, so each experiences the magnetic force $F = qvB$ directed along the rod; this drives electrons towards end $X$ and positive charge towards end $Y$, so charge separates, $X$ becomes negative and $Y$ becomes positive. The separation continues until the electric force $qE$ from the separated charge exactly balances the magnetic force, at which point the emf between the ends is $\varepsilon = vB \times$ (length of the rod).

Sub-part (i), one mark, is settled entirely by the vector product. The field in the gap runs from the $N$ face of the left magnet towards the $S$ face of the right magnet, so $\mathbf{B}$ is horizontal and directed to the right; the rod's velocity is vertically upward; and in the figure the rod recedes away from the viewer, so end $Y$ is the far end and end $X$ the end nearest the viewer. The current carriers in a metal are electrons, so $q$ is negative in $\mathbf{F} = q\mathbf{v}\times\mathbf{B}$, and with $\mathbf{v}$ up and $\mathbf{B}$ to the right the force on the electrons is along the rod towards end $X$. Electrons accumulate at $X$ and are removed from $Y$, so $X$ is negative and $Y$ positive. The two ways to lose this mark are to use $q$ as positive, and to take the external field as running from $S$ to $N$.

Sub-part (ii), three marks, needs a chain rather than a formula. The rod moves through the field, so the flux linking it changes with time, and the law of electromagnetic induction, $|\varepsilon| = N|\Delta\Phi/\Delta t|$, gives an emf. The microscopic account is that the free charge carriers are carried along with the rod, so each one moves through the field and experiences a magnetic force of magnitude $F = qvB$; because $\mathbf{v}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ are perpendicular, that force is directed along the rod rather than across it, and it drives electrons one way and positive carriers the other. Charge therefore separates inside the rod, $X$ negative and $Y$ positive, and the separation proceeds only until the electric force $qE$ it has created equals the magnetic force. Any one of three routes earns the full mark: reference to the change in flux, the separation-of-charge argument above, or the work done on the charges by the external agent moving the rod. A response that says only that an emf is produced by a change in flux, with no reference to this situation, earns one mark.

content.text: Explain how the principle of induction can be used to heat a conductor.

Two steps are needed and the question wants both. First ask what has to change for a current to be induced in a conductor at all; then ask what happens to that current in a conductor that has resistance.

There are two ways round the first step: put an alternating current in a fixed conductor, as in a transformer or an induction-coil supply, or keep the field fixed and move the conductor, as in an induction hob. Both change the flux through the conductor.

An alternating current is passed through the conductor, or the conductor is moved relative to a magnetic field (as in an induction hob). Either way the magnetic flux through the conductor changes, inducing a current in it. The induced current then meets the resistance of the conductor and dissipates energy as thermal energy, heating the conductor.

The first link is the induction itself: a changing magnetic flux through the conductor induces a current in it, with $|\varepsilon| = N|\Delta\Phi/\Delta t|$. This happens either because the flux is alternating, as in a transformer core or a mains-driven induction coil, or because the conductor moves relative to a static field, as in an induction hob. In both cases what matters is relative motion between the field and the conductor, and that is what changes the flux.

The second link is what turns the current into heat. The conductor has resistance, so the induced current meets that resistance and dissipates electrical energy as thermal energy, $P = I^{2}R$ or $Q = I^{2}Rt$, and that thermal energy is the heat. It is worth stating that the energy is transferred rather than created: the work done by whatever is changing the flux, the alternating source or the person moving the pan across the hob, is what pays for it. The rubric awards two marks for both links together and one mark for either alone, so an answer that describes induction without saying what happens to the current, or the reverse, earns one.

content.text: In terms of band structures and relative electrical resistance, describe the differences between a conductor, an insulator and a semiconductor.

Answer the question on the same three headings for each of the three materials: the arrangement of the valence and conduction bands, the number of mobile charge carriers available at room temperature, and the resulting resistance. Only then draw the comparison.

The clearest difference between a semiconductor and an insulator is quantitative rather than qualitative — the size of the energy gap — and remember that adding Group V or Group III impurities to a semiconductor changes the carrier population dramatically without changing its band structure. Note also that for a semiconductor the resistance falls as temperature rises, the opposite of a metal.

Conductors (metals): the valence band overlaps the conduction band, so there are large numbers of free electrons available at all temperatures; resistance is very low. Insulators: there is a large energy gap between the filled valence band and the empty conduction band, so thermal energy at room temperature cannot promote electrons and there are essentially no free charge carriers; resistance is extremely high. Semiconductors: there is a small energy gap between the valence and conduction bands; at ordinary temperatures a few electrons are thermally promoted across the gap, giving a small but increasing number of free electrons (and correspondingly holes), so the resistance is intermediate and falls as temperature rises. Doping (adding Group V or Group III impurities) greatly increases the number of free charge carriers and can produce n-type or p-type semiconductors with still lower resistance.
Compare the three on a common set of headings:

rows: The valence band overlaps or partly overlaps the conduction band, so the highest-energy electrons are delocalised at all temperatures

content.text: The differences follow directly from the band structure. A conductor has overlapping bands, so a large number of electrons is always available to move and the resistance is very low. content.text: Some materials become superconductors when cooled to extremely low temperatures.
Identify THREE properties of superconductors.
Start from what a current does in an ordinary conductor and consider what disappears if $R$ is exactly zero: no $I^{2}R$ heating, and therefore no limit on the current set by heating.

Look beyond the electrical property as well: one of the others is magnetic, and it is the one exploited when a vehicle is held clear of a track. A third concerns how much current the material can sustain compared with an ordinary conductor, which is why it is used in MRI scanners and accelerator magnets.

Zero electrical resistance: a superconductor carries current with no resistance, so no energy is lost as heat. Very large current-carrying capacity, allowing enormous currents to flow without melting the conductor. The Meissner effect: on cooling below the critical temperature the material expels magnetic field from its interior, which is why it can be used for magnetic levitation (and produces no $I^2R$ losses or frictional losses in a levitated system). Other accepted properties: a well-defined critical temperature below which the superconducting state is stable, and very small magnetic flux quantisation.
Three properties of superconductors below their critical temperature:

items: Zero electrical resistance. The resistance drops to exactly zero, so a current persists indefinitely in a closed loop and no energy is dissipated as heat, since $P = I^{2}R = 0$.

The Meissner effect. On cooling below the critical temperature the material expels magnetic field from its interior, so a superconductor is not merely a perfect conductor; this is what allows magnetic levitation and gives a levitated system no frictional losses.

Very high current-carrying capacity. Enormous current densities can be sustained without the material being destroyed by heating, which is why superconducting coils are used in MRI scanners and in the magnets of particle accelerators.

content.text: There are two areas in which energy savings can be made by the use of superconductors. These are:

- electricity generation and transmission;
- transportation.
Discuss how energy savings can be achieved in each of these two areas.
Handle the two areas separately, and in each one name the issue and then the energy consequence of removing that loss. Marks are awarded for the pairing, not for the feature on its own.

In the electricity area the superconducting machine has two distinct jobs: the windings of the generator lose no energy to heat, and the lines that carry the current lose none either. In transportation the relevant property is the one that removes friction at the contact surface.

Electricity generation: superconductor windings in generators allow much larger currents, so a smaller, lighter generator can deliver the same power; with zero resistance no energy is wasted as heat in the windings, so less fuel must be burnt to produce the same electrical energy. Transmission: with zero resistance there are no $I^2R$ losses in the transmission lines, so much less energy is lost between the power station and the consumer, and power can be transmitted over greater distances; combined with efficient step-up transformers this allows high-voltage transmission with minimal line heating, so less generating capacity is needed to replace losses. Transportation: magnetic levitation (Maglev) trains use the Meissner effect to levitate the vehicle, so there is no contact friction between vehicle and track; the energy normally wasted overcoming friction is saved, less force is needed to accelerate the train and it can travel faster on less energy.
Electricity generation and transmission:

items: Generation: superconducting windings have zero resistance, so no energy is wasted as heat in the rotor and stator. Less fuel must be burnt in the turbine to produce the same electrical energy, and the machine runs cool so it needs less cooling.
Generation: because the windings tolerate very large currents, a smaller and lighter generator can deliver the same power, so less material is used and the machine's own losses are reduced.

Transmission: a superconducting line has no $I^{2}R$ loss, so almost none of the energy generated is lost between the power station and the consumer, and power can be sent over much greater distances without an unacceptable loss fraction.

content.text: Transportation:

items: A maglev train is levitated using the Meissner effect, so there is no mechanical contact between the vehicle and the track. The energy that would be dissipated overcoming friction is therefore saved.
Because frictional losses are removed, less driving force is needed to accelerate the train and the same energy input produces a higher speed, so the energy used per unit distance falls.

content.text: Describe Earth's current magnetic field.
Two features of the anomaly pattern need separate explanations: why the bands alternate, and why the pattern is symmetrical about the ridge axis.

Think about what happens to a newly formed ocean crust as it cools, about what happens to the direction of Earth's field over geological time, and about what carries the record of both away from the ridge.

The field is approximately dipolar rather than uniform, with curved field lines that leave the Earth near the geographic south pole and enter it near the geographic north pole (so the geographic north pole behaves as a magnetic south pole). The axis of the dipolar field is tilted about $11.5^{\circ}$ to the rotational axis, the field lines are directed out of the Earth in the southern hemisphere and into it in the northern hemisphere, and the field strength is greatest at the poles and weakest at the equator, being about twice as strong at the poles as at the equator.

The key is that rock can record the direction of a magnetic field as it cools. Iron-bearing minerals in basalt become magnetised in the direction of the ambient field as the temperature falls through the Curie point, and that direction is then fixed for the life of the rock. At a mid-ocean ridge new crust is continuously created and pushed aside, so a sequence of such records is laid down parallel to the ridge. Whenever the field reverses, the next band is magnetised the opposite way, which is exactly what the alternating light and dark bands in the diagram represent. The symmetry about the ridge follows because each piece of crust is split by the spreading and carried away equally in both directions, and the increasing separation of matching bands with distance from the ridge shows that spreading has not proceeded at a constant rate.

content.text: The diagram represents the magnetic anomalies of the oceanic crust located near the island of Iceland in the mid-Atlantic. Explain the origin of the pattern of magnetic anomalies on either side of the mid-ocean ridge.

Magma wells up at the mid-ocean ridge and solidifies to form new ocean crust. As the iron-rich minerals in the crust cool through the Curie temperature they align with the field existing at that moment and are permanently magnetised in that direction. Because the field has reversed many times in Earth's history, bands formed during normal polarity and bands formed during reversed polarity alternate along the ridge, producing the black and white pattern. Crust formed at the same time is carried equally far to each side, so the pattern is symmetrical about the ridge, and the bands become progressively wider and further apart with distance from the ridge, showing that the rate of sea-floor spreading has not been constant.

content.text: Recount the steps involved in gravity data reduction.
A gravity reading taken at the surface is not a direct measure of anything beneath it: it has to be corrected first. Part (i) is a recall of those corrections, in the order in which they are applied.

For (ii)(1), remember that the anomaly is what is left after the corrections, so it reflects the density of the rock beneath the station, and that the water in a sea is far less dense than the rock it lies on. Read the anomaly curve at the two marked positions before interpreting anything.
For (ii)(2), a satellite in a circular orbit is falling, so relate the radius of its path to the local value of $g$ at the point it is passing over.

Determine the latitude, longitude and elevation of each gravity station; calculate the theoretical (normal) gravity for that latitude and elevation; apply the free-air correction for the station's height above the geoid; apply the Bouguer correction for the mass of rock between the station and the datum; apply the terrain correction for the attraction of nearby topography. The corrected value is then compared with the normal gravity value to obtain the gravity anomaly at that station.

A gravimeter measures the attraction of everything below it, so its raw reading is the sum of the normal field and an anomaly caused by the local geology. Reduction is the sequence of corrections that removes the effects which can be calculated in advance: latitude, free-air, Bouguer and terrain. What survives is the gravity anomaly, a measure of how the density of the rock beneath the station differs from the standard crust.

content.text: (i) P waves are longitudinal (compressional) and travel about twice as fast as S waves, so they arrive first at every distance; S waves are transverse (shear). P waves travel through both solids and liquids whereas S waves need a medium with shear strength and so travel only through solids.

(ii) Beyond about $11\,000\,\mathrm{km}$ the direct S wave path from the epicentre passes through the liquid outer core. A liquid has no rigidity and cannot support a transverse wave, so the S waves are absorbed there, leaving an S wave shadow zone and no S arrivals on the far side of the Earth.

(iii) Both the direct P and the direct S lines stop at about $11\,000\,\mathrm{km}$, because beyond that distance the direct path enters the core and the waves are refracted sharply away from the observer. P waves reappear only at much later times along two branches, $P'$ and $P''$: $P'$ has been refracted through the liquid outer core, and $P''$ has been reflected from a boundary of finite radius inside it, which can only be a solid inner core. The delayed, refracted and reflected P arrivals in the 11 000 km to 16 000 km range therefore demonstrate a solid inner core bounded by the liquid outer core.

content.text: Assess the application and advantages of TWO geophysical methods in mineral exploration.
Choose two methods that respond to different physical properties, so that you can compare what each can and cannot detect.

For each method be ready to give the physical principle, what is actually measured, the kind of deposit it suits, and at least one limitation; an assessment needs the comparison as well as the description.
Finish with a judgement about how the two methods are used together in practice, rather than two unrelated descriptions.

Seismic refraction/reflection surveying: explosive or vibrator sources generate elastic waves that are refracted at boundaries between layers of different wave speed and reflected from them; the travel times are recorded by geophones and interpreted to give a velocity-versus-depth profile. Because the velocity of a wave depends on the elasticity and density of the rock, an anomaly in velocity identifies a change of rock type, so the technique maps the depth and shape of a sedimentary basin or an ore body accurately. Its advantage is that it gives detailed information about the depth and three-dimensional structure of a deposit, which gravity and magnetic surveys cannot, but it is expensive, requires drilling or explosive access, and is slow. Magnetic surveying: the Earth's field magnetises minerals such as magnetite, and a magnetometer is used to detect the small anomalies in the total magnetic field caused by buried ore bodies. Because magnetite and some sulphide ores are strongly magnetic, the method is cheap, rapid and can be flown as an airborne survey over large inaccessible areas, but it responds only to magnetically responsive minerals, gives no information about depth, and is easily confused with the magnetic effects of the underlying igneous basement, so it identifies targets for further testing rather than proving the presence of an ore body. Together the methods are complementary: the broad, rapid magnetic survey locates likely targets and the slower, more expensive seismic survey then evaluates them in detail.

Seismic surveying sends a controlled elastic wave, from an explosive or a vibrator truck, into the ground and records the arrival times at geophones. Waves are reflected from, and refracted at, boundaries where the wave speed changes, and because the speed depends on the elasticity and density of the rock, the travel-time data give a velocity-versus-depth profile that maps the depth and three-dimensional shape of a deposit. It is the most detailed of the methods but it is expensive, slow and needs access for the source. Magnetic surveying measures the small anomalies in the Earth's field produced by magnetised minerals such as magnetite; it is cheap, rapid and can be flown, so it surveys enormous areas quickly, but it responds only to magnetically susceptible minerals, gives no depth information and is easily confused with the magnetic effects of the basement. The judgement that follows is that the broad, cheap magnetic survey is used first to identify targets over a large area, and the slower, more expensive seismic survey is then used to evaluate those targets in detail.

content.text: Briefly describe how an endoscope works.
Part (i) is about how a bundle of optical fibres can carry both light and an image. Think about what happens to light at a glass-air boundary when the angle of incidence is large enough.

Part (ii) is about producing a two-dimensional image from one-dimensional measurements. Ask what a single X-ray photograph of the body can and cannot tell you, and what has to be varied to get around that.

An endoscope is a thin flexible tube containing bundles of optical fibres. Light from an external lamp is guided down one bundle to the tip by repeated total internal reflection, a lens at the tip forms an image of the organ being examined, and that image is carried back along a second bundle, again by total internal reflection, to be viewed through an eyepiece.

Both techniques exist to overcome the limitations of a single straight line of sight. In the endoscope the geometry problem is solved by bending the light path: a fibre optic works by total internal reflection, so any light entering one fibre at more than the critical angle is trapped inside it and guided along its length. That allows a bundle of thousands of fibres to be routed around a corner into the body, and a second bundle to bring the image back out, so the interior can be seen without an incision. In the CAT scan the problem is different: a single X-ray transmission image is a superposition of everything along one line, so different structures overlap. Rotating the source and detectors around the patient gives many different projections of the same slice, and because the computer knows where the source and detectors were for each projection it can solve backwards for the absorption of each small region of the slice, producing a cross-sectional image and, by stacking slices, a three-dimensional reconstruction.

content.text: Explain how a computed axial tomography (CAT) scan is produced.

An X-ray tube is rotated around the patient so a narrow beam passes through the body from many different angles while detectors on the far side measure the transmitted intensity. Different tissues absorb X-rays by different amounts according to their density and thickness, so the detector reading varies with angle. A computer combines the many projections mathematically and reconstructs a cross-sectional image of the slice being scanned; a series of slices can be combined to give a three-dimensional view.

Before choosing a scan, list what each of the three techniques uses (X-rays, sound, a strong magnetic field) and what that implies about the risk to the patient.

For (i) you are comparing an MRI with a CAT scan, so compare them on the same criteria: radiation risk, contrast between soft tissues, procedure time and cost. For (ii) you are given a specific clinical question, whether there is a break in the bone, so ask which imaging method shows bone best and which is quickest and safest for that.
For (iii) the question has moved from bone to brain tissue, so choose the scan that images soft tissue best and justify the choice against the alternatives.

items: (i) MRI uses no ionising radiation, so there is no risk of damaging cells or of increasing cancer risk, which makes it much safer for children and pregnant women; and it gives far better contrast between soft tissues such as muscle, brain, ligaments and tumours than a CAT scan, so it shows detail a CAT scan cannot. It can also image in any plane without moving the patient and needs no contrast medium.

(ii) X-rays are strongly absorbed by dense material such as bone, so bone appears as a distinct white region against the darker soft tissue. A fracture breaks the continuity of the bone and fills the gap with less dense material, so it appears as a dark line through the white bone. An X-ray is also quick (about 5 minutes), cheap, widely available and involves only a small radiation dose, which makes it the appropriate first test for a suspected fracture.

(iii) A CAT scan or an MRI scan of the head. A CAT scan is quick, uses a low dose of X-rays and shows whether the fractured bone has been driven inwards towards the brain; an MRI images the brain itself with high contrast, showing bruising, bleeding and diffuse injury without ionising radiation.

content.text: The choice of imaging technique follows from what the clinician needs to know and from what the physics of each technique makes visible. X-rays are absorbed in proportion to the density and thickness of the material they pass through, so dense bone stands out white against soft tissue; that is exactly the contrast needed to look for a break in a skull, and because bone is so much denser than the material that replaces it in a fracture, the fracture appears as a dark line. X-rays are also the fastest and cheapest of the three, which is why they are the first test for a suspected fracture. For the brain, however, the contrast that distinguishes bone is useless, because a CAT scan shows brain tissue poorly. An MRI places the patient in a strong magnetic field, aligns the hydrogen nuclei in the tissue, tips them with a radio-frequency pulse and detects the radio waves they emit as they relax; the signal depends on the density and chemical environment of the hydrogen, so soft tissues that look identical on an X-ray are clearly distinguished. Its disadvantages are the 30 to 60 minutes the patient must lie still in a narrow magnet, its cost, and the fact that it cannot image bone as well as an X-ray, which is precisely why a patient needing both a skull and a brain assessment has both tests.

content.text: Assess the impact of medical applications based on ultrasound and the magnetic field of particles within the body on modern society.
An assessment needs more than a list of uses: for each application say what the physics allows it to do, what benefit that brings to patients, and what limits its use.

Look for the trade-offs the question is inviting you to weigh, such as cost, procedure time, the need for the patient to cooperate, and restrictions on what can be implanted or used near the machine, and be explicit about who is affected by them.
Finish with an overall judgement, including who gains most from these techniques and where they are still not available.

Ultrasound (high frequency sound waves, typically 1–20 MHz) is used diagnostically to image the fetus during pregnancy, to examine the heart (echocardiography) and blood vessels (Doppler ultrasound), the eye, the abdomen and the brain. Sound waves are reflected at boundaries between tissues of different acoustic impedance; because the speed of sound in tissue is about 1500 m/s, the depth of each boundary is calculated from the echo time. Its impact has been enormous: it has made antenatal care safe and routine, it allows heart valves and blood flow to be monitored without surgery, it enables biopsy of internal organs without opening the body, and because it uses sound rather than ionising radiation it can be used repeatedly, on children and on pregnant women, with no known harmful effects. MRI uses the magnetic field of the nuclei of hydrogen atoms in the body: hydrogen nuclei in a strong field behave as tiny magnets that precess at the Larmor frequency, a radio-frequency pulse tips them over, and the radio waves emitted as they relax are detected and used to construct an image. MRI has given clinicians high-contrast images of soft tissue that no X-ray technique can provide, revolutionising the diagnosis and management of brain tumours, multiple sclerosis, ligament and spinal cord injuries, and joint damage. The limitations to weigh are cost: MRI scanners are far more expensive than X-ray or ultrasound equipment, so they are not available in all hospitals or in rural areas; scans are slow (30–60 minutes) and the patient must lie very still in a narrow, noisy, confining magnet, which is distressing for children and claustrophobic patients and makes monitoring difficult for very sick patients; strong magnetic fields restrict the use of implants and require screening; and MRI cannot show bone as clearly as an X-ray. Overall both applications have substantially improved the diagnosis of disease at far lower risk to patients than exploratory surgery, but access to the more expensive of the two is still uneven, and the presence of the older, cheaper X-ray technique means that all three remain in use.

Ultrasound sends high-frequency sound into the body and listens to the echoes from boundaries between tissues of different acoustic impedance. Because the speed of sound in tissue is roughly constant at about $1500\,\mathrm{m/s}$, the echo time gives the depth of each boundary, so the returning echoes build up a cross-sectional image without any radiation. Its impact has been extensive: routine antenatal imaging, echocardiography and Doppler measurement of blood flow, biopsy of internal organs without surgery, all repeatable on children and pregnant women because sound causes no ionising damage. MRI works on the magnetic behaviour of the hydrogen nuclei in the body: in a strong field the nuclei align, a radio-frequency pulse tips them, and the radio waves they emit as they relax are detected and mapped into an image. Because the signal depends on the chemical environment of the hydrogen, MRI resolves soft tissue detail that no X-ray technique can show, which has transformed the management of brain tumours, multiple sclerosis, ligament and spinal-cord injury and joint damage. The limitations must be weighed against those benefits: MRI scanners are far more expensive than X-ray or ultrasound equipment and are not evenly distributed, particularly in rural areas; the 30 to 60 minute scan in a narrow, noisy magnet is distressing for children and claustrophobic patients and prevents continuous monitoring of very sick patients; ferromagnetic implants must be excluded by screening; and bone is still imaged better by X-ray. The overall judgement is that both applications have made diagnosis far safer and far more informative than exploratory surgery, and that the older, cheaper X-ray technique therefore remains in use alongside them.

content.text: Binary stars are important in determining stellar masses.
Explain how the total mass of a binary star system can be calculated.

The orbital period $T$ is measured from the periodic change in brightness or from the Doppler shifts of the spectral lines, and the separation $r$ of the two stars from the observed orbital motion of those lines, or from astrometry combined with the distance. Applying Kepler's third law to the motion of the two stars about their common centre of mass gives $M_{1} + M_{2} = \dfrac{4\pi^{2}r^{3}}{GT^{2}}$, and the ratio of the two orbital radii then gives the mass ratio and hence the individual masses.

the separation of the two stars is found from the astrometric or spectroscopic orbit, and Kepler's third law for a two-body system, which compares the period with the size of the orbit about the centre of mass, gives the total mass directly because the gravitational constant and the measured $r$ and $T$ are all known. The mass ratio from the ratio of the two orbital radii then separates that total into the two stellar masses.

content.text: For (i) decide what two properties a white dwarf has, how small it is and how hot it is, and use $L = 4\pi R^{2}\sigma T^{4}$ to work out which corner of the diagram that puts it in. Read the axes of the printed diagram carefully, because the temperature scale runs backwards.

items: (i) Position S. White dwarfs are the exposed cores of low-mass stars that have exhausted their fuel, so they are small and have cooled to a few thousand kelvin, giving a very low luminosity (about $10^{-2}$ to $10^{-1}$ solar luminosities); this places them in the lower left of the diagram, well away from the main sequence.

(ii) A white dwarf has no nuclear fuel, so there is no fusion pressure to hold it up and gravity would otherwise make it contract. Its density is so high, however, that the electrons are forced into a very small volume, and because no two electrons can occupy the same quantum state (Pauli exclusion principle) the resulting electron degeneracy pressure rises steeply as the star contracts. It rises until it exactly balances gravity, so the star is in hydrostatic equilibrium and no longer shrinks.

(iii) $4\,{}^{1}_{1}\mathrm{H} \longrightarrow {}^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He} + 2\,{}^{0}_{+1}\mathrm{e} + 2\nu + \text{energy}$ (about $26\,\mathrm{MeV}$), the proton-proton chain that powers a main-sequence star.

content.text: The H-R diagram plots luminosity against surface temperature, and luminosity follows from the radius and the temperature, so a star's position is fixed by those two quantities. A white dwarf is the remnant core of a low-mass star: very small in radius and only moderately hot, so $L = 4\pi R^{2}\sigma T^{4}$ is tiny and the star lies in the cool, dim region away from the main sequence, which is position S. Its stability is a different question. With no fuel there is no fusion, so the only support against gravity comes from the electrons: at white-dwarf densities the electrons are forced by the Pauli exclusion principle into a very small volume, and the resulting degeneracy pressure is extremely stiff, increasing so rapidly with compression that it balances gravity at a fixed radius. For (iii) the main sequence is powered by hydrogen fusion, the proton-proton chain, in which four hydrogen nuclei combine to form one helium-4 nucleus with the release of about 26 MeV of energy, together with two positrons and two neutrinos.

content.text: Discuss how the development of adaptive optics and at least one other development have improved resolution and sensitivity of ground based astronomy.

Start by being precise about the two things being improved: resolution is the ability to separate two nearby sources, and sensitivity is the ability to detect a faint source. They have different causes and different cures.

For resolution, work out what limits a ground-based telescope: the aperture sets one floor and the atmosphere sets a much worse one. Then ask how each development attacks that particular limit. For sensitivity, ask how much light is collected and how efficiently it is recorded.
A strong response weighs the developments against each other and against what still limits ground-based astronomy, rather than simply listing them.

Resolution is the ability to distinguish two objects that are close together, and is limited for a ground based telescope by diffraction (which sets a floor related to the aperture) and, much more seriously, by atmospheric 'seeing' — the turbulent, moving layers of air in the atmosphere distort and smear the light from a star, so a star that should be a point appears as a fluctuating blurred disc of perhaps an arcsecond across. Sensitivity is the ability to detect faint sources, which depends on how much light can be collected (the area of the aperture) and on the noise in the recording. Adaptive optics is a development that addresses seeing: a wavefront sensor measures the distortions of the incoming light many hundreds of times per second, a computer calculates the corrections needed, and a small flexible mirror (or a set of mirror segments) in the telescope is deformed rapidly to exactly cancel the atmospheric distortion. The star image is then as sharp as if there were no atmosphere, so the angular resolution approaches the diffraction limit of the telescope, allowing close double stars to be separated and planets to be detected near their parent stars. Three other developments have improved resolution and sensitivity: larger mirrors (for example the 8.1 m Very Large Telescope) collect proportionally more light, so fainter objects are detected (greater sensitivity) and the diffraction limit is finer (greater resolution); interferometry, in which the light from several widely separated telescopes is combined, gives a baseline far larger than any single dish and so much finer resolution, and the Very Large Array extended radio astronomy to arcsecond and better resolution; and the replacement of photographic plates by cooled CCD cameras, which convert far more of the arriving photons into recorded data, greatly increase sensitivity and allow shorter exposures. The trade-off is that these developments are extremely expensive and complex, so they are available only at a few sites, while the atmosphere still limits what ground based instruments can achieve compared with a space telescope above the atmosphere.

Resolution and sensitivity fail for different reasons, and the developments in this question address them separately. Seeing, not diffraction, is the dominant limit on the resolution of a ground-based telescope: turbulence in the atmosphere distorts the wavefront from a star so that a point source is recorded as a fluctuating blurred disc of order an arcsecond. Adaptive optics attacks that directly, with a wavefront sensor measuring the incoming distortions many hundreds of times a second, a computer calculating the correction required, and a small flexible mirror deformed to cancel the distortion, so the recorded image is as sharp as it would be in space and the resolution approaches the diffraction limit set by the aperture. The other developments improve what the telescope can do even in ideal conditions: a larger mirror collects proportionally more light, which raises sensitivity and also lowers the diffraction limit $1.22\lambda/D$; interferometry replaces a single aperture with a baseline far greater than any single dish, giving correspondingly finer resolution; and cooled CCD cameras record a far larger fraction of the arriving photons than photographic plates, so fainter objects are detected and exposures can be shorter. The trade-offs are cost and complexity, and the atmosphere still sets the ultimate limit for any ground-based instrument.

For (ii), start from de Broglie's relation and ask what has to be true about the circumference of the orbit if the electron is to be a stationary state. Then show that this condition is equivalent to Bohr's quantum condition on angular momentum.

Davisson and Germer directed a beam of electrons, accelerated through a potential difference, at a single crystal of nickel. They measured the intensity of the electrons scattered at different angles from the crystal with a movable detector. The scattered intensity showed a clear diffraction pattern with a maximum, and the angles of the maxima were in close agreement with the angles predicted for the diffraction of a wave of wavelength $\lambda = h/(mv)$ for the electrons used, so the electron diffraction confirms the wave nature of electrons and de Broglie's hypothesis.

content.text: Explain the stability of the electron orbits in the Bohr atom, using de Broglie's hypothesis.

De Broglie's hypothesis gives every particle of mass $m$ moving at speed $v$ an associated wavelength $\lambda = h/(mv)$, so the electron in orbit may be described as a wave travelling round the nucleus. If only a fraction of a wavelength fitted into the circumference the wave would interfere with itself and be destroyed, so the orbit can be a stationary state only when a whole number of wavelengths fits: $2\pi r = n\lambda$. The electron is then a standing wave with fixed nodes and does not radiate, so classical theory's collapse into the nucleus does not occur, and the condition is exactly $mvr = nh/2\pi = n\hbar$, i.e. the angular momentum is quantised. Because $n$ must be a whole number the electron can occupy only certain discrete orbits and the atom is stable.

: the standing-wave condition gives the quantised angular momentum directly, which is Bohr's second postulate recovered from de Broglie's hypothesis. The two common failures are to write $2\pi r = n\lambda$ and then stop (never reaching the quantisation of $L$), and to omit the reason the number of wavelengths must be an integer - without it the wave self-destructs and the argument for stability is lost.

content.text: Account for the energy distribution of electrons.

If the nucleus emitted a single particle its electrons would all have the same energy, as in alpha decay. Instead the graph shows a continuous distribution from zero up to a definite end-point of about $1.2\,\mathrm{MeV}$, because the electron does not carry away all the available energy: a second particle, the neutrino, is emitted at the same time, is electrically neutral and has negligible mass, and carries away the balance of the energy and momentum. The end-point is the rare case in which the neutrino carries away almost no energy, so the electron has the maximum possible kinetic energy, equal to the full energy released by the mass defect.

Momentum conservation also has to be satisfied by the products, and the electron alone cannot carry the momentum required by the collision, so a second particle must exist. It must be neutral, because no ionisation accompanies the decay, and of negligible mass, because the end-point equals the whole of the Q-value.

content.text: Look at which energy level every one of the four lines has in common. Once that is identified the series is fully defined and the wavelength of any line is fixed by the difference between that level and the upper level.

The four lines shown come from upper levels of 3, 4, 5 and 6, so the next line comes from the next whole number. Use $\frac{1}{\lambda} = R\left(\frac{1}{n_f^{2}} - \frac{1}{n_i^{2}}\right)$ with $R = 1.097\times10^{7}\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}$.
Part (i) is an argument, not a description: state what Bohr's model predicts, state what is observed, and then say why no competing model could produce that result.

(i) Bohr's model restricts the electron of the hydrogen atom to certain discrete energy levels. When an electron falls from a higher level to the $n = 2$ level a single photon is emitted with energy $E = hf$ equal to the difference between the two levels, so instead of a continuous spectrum only a small number of discrete wavelengths can be produced. The Balmer series is exactly this set of transitions - electrons dropping to $n = 2$ from $n = 3, 4, 5, 6$ - giving the four observed lines at $656\,\mathrm{nm}$, $486\,\mathrm{nm}$, $434\,\mathrm{nm}$ and $410\,\mathrm{nm}$, and the wavelengths calculated from Bohr's levels agree closely with the observed values. A classical model can predict neither the existence of discrete lines nor their precise wavelengths, so the agreement is strong experimental evidence for Bohr's quantised energy levels. (ii) $\lambda = 3.97\times10^{-7}\,\mathrm{m}$ ($397\,\mathrm{nm}$), the $H_{\varepsilon}$ line from $n = 7 \rightarrow 2$.
All four visible Balmer lines end at the same level, $n = 2$; the upper levels are 3, 4, 5, 6.

Two traps here. The formula gives $1/\lambda$, so the final step must be an inversion, not a multiplication. And the bracket is the difference of two reciprocals, $0.25 - 0.02041$, not $0.25 \times 0.02041$: taking it as about $0.205$ gives $445\,\mathrm{nm}$, which is not a Balmer wavelength at all.

For (i), the strength of the evidence lies in the lines being discrete and quantitatively predicted. Rutherford's nuclear model and a classical orbit both give a continuous range of possible energies, so neither can produce four lines at the wavelengths observed; only quantised levels can, and they predict them quantitatively.

content.text: Discuss how neutron scattering and ONE other process have been used to increase our understanding of the structure of matter.

The marking scheme rewards a logical discussion, not two unrelated descriptions, so fix the plan first: for each process say what is sent in, what it interacts with, what is measured, and what can be concluded about structure from that measurement.

For each process also give one piece of evidence about the structure of matter that it produced and one modern use. The 'one other process' is your choice - X-ray diffraction, electron diffraction and alpha-particle scattering all qualify.

Neutron scattering: a beam of neutrons is directed at a sample and the angles and intensities of the scattered neutrons are measured. A neutron carries no electric charge, so it is not deflected by the atomic nuclei in the way an alpha particle is; it interacts only with the nuclei through the strong nuclear force, and because the nuclear force is very short range, a neutron is diffracted only by structures of comparable size to the nucleus. The resulting diffraction pattern is the Fourier transform of the nuclear density of the sample. This is why neutrons, rather than X-rays or alpha particles, reveal the position of nuclei: the first experiments in the 1930s, and the later neutron diffraction experiments, showed that the atom contains a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus with a radius of order $10^{-15}\,\mathrm{m}$, and established the scale of nuclear and atomic structure; neutron scattering is still used today to determine the positions of hydrogen atoms in biological molecules and in the crystal structure of materials. One other process: X-ray diffraction. When a beam of X-rays of a known wavelength is scattered by the regularly spaced atoms of a crystal, the angles of the diffraction maxima give, by Bragg's law $n\lambda = 2d\sin\theta$, the spacing $d$ of the atomic planes. This allowed the arrangement of atoms in crystals to be mapped in three dimensions, confirming the wave nature of X-rays, giving the Avogadro number and confirming the wave nature of light, and ultimately leading to the structure of DNA and of proteins. The two processes are complementary: X-rays probe the electron density and are strongest for heavy atoms, whereas neutrons probe the nuclear density and are sensitive to light atoms such as hydrogen; using both, together with electron diffraction, has made it possible to determine the structure of matter from the atomic to the nuclear scale, which is essential to the understanding of the properties of materials and of biological molecules.

Plan the answer as a comparison with a closing judgement, not as two separate essays. For each of the two processes take the same four headings: probe and what it interacts with; the measurement and the law used to extract structure; the structural conclusion and the evidence for it; one present-day application.

items: Neutron scattering: uncharged neutron beam, interacts with nuclei through the short-range strong force only; diffraction angles and intensities measured; nuclear density of the sample mapped.

X-ray diffraction: X-rays scattered by the regularly spaced atoms of a crystal; maxima at $n\lambda = 2d\sin\theta$ give the spacing $d$ of the atomic planes; atomic arrangements mapped in three dimensions.

Close by naming what each probe is blind to: X-rays scatter from electrons and so are strongest for heavy atoms, while neutrons scatter from nuclei and are sensitive to light atoms such as hydrogen. State explicitly that the two fill in each other's gaps.
Finish with a single judgement sentence, e.g. that our picture of matter from the atomic to the nuclear scale rests on several complementary probes rather than on one.

content.text: Describe the structure of an LED. (2 marks)
Structure means the layers and the junction: what has been doped to make a p-type layer and an n-type layer, where the two meet, and how the package is built around them.

The phrase 'rather than an ordinary light source' tells you the second sub-part is a list of advantages, and the marking guide awards a mark for each advantage described - four are needed for full marks.

An LED is a solid-state diode consisting of a chip of semiconductor, usually gallium arsenide or gallium phosphide, that has been doped to form two layers in contact, a p-type layer and an n-type layer, creating a p-n junction. The junction is mounted in a reflector inside a transparent plastic or epoxy casing and leads connect to the two layers. When the LED is forward biased, electrons are pushed from the n-type layer into the p-type layer, recombine with holes, and the energy released appears as photons of a characteristic colour, so the light is emitted at the junction.

The mechanism must include forward bias, electrons crossing from the n-type to the p-type layer, recombination with holes, and the released energy leaving as photons of a characteristic wavelength set by the band gap.

content.text: Explain why, in some applications, it is preferable to use an LED rather than an ordinary light source. (4 marks)

LEDs are far more efficient, converting a much larger fraction of the supplied electrical energy into light, so they run cool and consume very little power and the running cost is low; they have a very long working life, tens of thousands of hours, and degrade gradually rather than failing suddenly, so maintenance costs are low; they are small, light and rugged, with no fragile glass envelope or hot filament, so they can be built into compact equipment and survive vibration and impact; they switch on and off instantly with no warm-up time and can be dimmed; they operate from low-voltage DC so no transformer is needed; and the emitted colour can be chosen, or the emission taken into the infrared, without the cost and bulk of filters.

The four most reliable are efficiency (including low heat and low running cost), long predictable life, small robust construction, and instant switching on low-voltage DC. content.text: Describe the properties of an ideal amplifier.
Identify the region of the table where the output changes by a constant amount for a constant change in the input. Only that region can be used to define a gain; the ends of the table cannot.
Work in volts for the output and convert the microvolt input to volts before dividing, then check the power of ten in the result.
The last sub-part is about the edges of the table, not the middle: compare what the linear gain predicts with what the table actually shows at the largest inputs.

An ideal amplifier has an infinitely high input resistance, so it draws no current from the signal source and does not load or alter the input; zero output resistance, so the output is not affected by the load connected to it; infinite voltage gain, so the output is an exact inverted multiple of the input; and no noise, no distortion and no loss of signal, so the output is an undistorted amplified copy of the input with the same shape.
The straight part of the table runs from $-150$ to $+150$ microvolt, where the output changes by a constant $2.0\,\mathrm{V}$ for every $50$ microvolt of input.

The same magnitude follows from any other pair of points on the straight part of the table, for example $+6.0/(150\times10^{-6}) = 4.0\times10^{4}$ and $-2.0/(-50\times10^{-6}) = 4.0\times10^{4}$, which is the check that the value is a constant gain. The negative sign is not a sign error: the output is $180^{\circ}$ out of phase with the input, so the amplifier inverts.

From the table the output stops changing once $|V_{\text{in}}|$ reaches about 200 microvolt, so the amplifier saturates there. Two limits are therefore in play - the maximum output voltage and the size of the input signal - and both must be named for the second mark in sub-part

content.text: Early computers used thermionic devices. Later computers used transistors and today computers use integrated circuits. Discuss the impact and limitations of these developments.

Work generation by generation. For each of valves, transistors and integrated circuits write the limitation of that technology first, then the impact the next technology had on computers, then the new limitation it created.
The marking scheme awards marks for linking the developments to the older technology, so avoid three separate descriptions with no connection drawn between them.

Thermionic valves (triodes, invented in the 1940s) made electronic computation possible, but a single valve was large, generated much heat, needed a high heater power, had a warm-up time, was fragile and had a limited life, and a computer needed tens of thousands of them, so machines were enormous, slow and enormously expensive to run and to maintain. The first major impact of the change was the transistor (1947), which is a small, cheap, robust, low-power solid-state switch with no moving parts and no warm-up time. Thousands of transistors replaced millions of valves, so computers became far smaller, faster, cheaper and more reliable, and for the first time computers could be used in business and homes. The limitation of a discrete transistor is that each one performs only one function, so a large computer still needed thousands of individually wired components, and interconnection and assembly dominated cost and reliability. The integrated circuit (invented 1958, silicon 1960s) put many transistors, and later millions, together with their interconnections on a single chip of silicon. This had a dramatic impact: the number of components on a chip doubled roughly every two years, so the same performance was obtained from ever smaller and cheaper machines, giving microprocessors, computers small enough to fit in a watch, and enormously greater speed and storage. The limitations of the integrated circuit are heat dissipation, since the chips run hot and must be cooled; the limits of the purity and size of the silicon crystal and of the lithographic patterning, which have now been approached; the fact that fabrication plants cost billions of dollars, so only a few manufacturers can produce leading chips, creating dependence on a small number of companies; and continuing difficulties in disposing of the enormous quantities of obsolete hardware. Each development solved the limitations of its predecessor — solid state replaced the hot fragile valve, and integration replaced the wired discrete transistor — and each has also created new problems, so the direction of progress is set by overcoming the limitations of the previous technology while increasing both speed and the amount of information that can be processed.

items: Set out a three-column plan: device, limitation of that device, what the next device solved and what limitation it introduced in turn.

Valves: a heated cathode in an evacuated glass envelope; large and bulky, long warm-up time, high heater power, much heat, stray magnetic fields, fragile, limited life, and tens of thousands were needed, so machines were enormous, slow and very expensive to run.

Transistors (1947): solid state, no heated cathode, no vacuum, no moving parts; tiny, cheap, robust, low power, instantaneous switching and long life, so machines became far smaller, faster, cheaper and more reliable. New limitation: each device performs only one function, so thousands of individually wired components were still needed and interconnection dominated cost and reliability.

Integrated circuits (Kilby 1958, planar silicon 1959, commercial from the mid-1960s): many transistors and their interconnections fabricated on a single chip of silicon; the number of components per area roughly doubled every two years, giving microprocessors and computers small enough to fit in a watch. New limitations: heat dissipation, the limits of silicon crystal purity and size and of lithographic patterning, the billion-dollar cost of fabrication plants, and disposal of obsolete hardware.
Close with a judgement sentence that ties the three together: each technology removed its predecessor's binding limitation while raising speed and information density.
